Second, it seems to me that the clientele who invest in annuities would have a new option in investing their RRSP. There is a whole clientele of taxpayers who would love to take part in an annuity program if they knew where that money was going. At present, when they go through a bank or an insurance company they know very well that the money will be reinvested but they have no control over the reinvestment program-that is the option of the credit union or bank. I am thinking of people with very strong religious convictions, for example, who do not necessarily want their money invested in liquor companies, distilleries or tobacco companies but would gladly invest their money in an RRSP if they knew that the annuity in the end could be turned over to a charitable organization, a church, a university, the YMCA, or mission programs.
If the government would liberalize this aspect of it, I think they would be doing a service to the taxpayer which has not been available up to the present time. I wonder if the minister, to whom I mentioned this a couple of years ago, would entertain this kind of flexibility for the taxpayer which would allow him to invest in this program with some knowledge of where his money is being invested, and let him live with his conscience this way.

I think we have to keep in mind the purpose of an RRSP. It is an investment, and we are giving an opportunity to a person to put aside some of his earnings for his retirement time. We propose here the addition of the RR1F which adds flexibility to the program by allowing a person, when he reaches the age of 71, to choose either to buy a life annuity or to cash in his RRSP. What the hon. member is suggesting is that we should permit people to invest in religious organizations, the YMCA, universities, and so on. What we are trying to achieve is to make sure that the money put aside by people making those savings is guaranteed so that when their time of retirement comes the money will be there. It is always possible to give money to charitable organizations, but I do not think it would be wise to invest it in this case because it might lead to all sorts of problems.
Suppose that someone decided that his RRSP should be invested in the YMCA, but it turns out that in 20 years' time the YMCA in Ottawa goes bankrupt. The poor man, who had decided to invest in this organization, would find that it could not deliver his money at the end of the process. That is why we are asking financial institutions with a sound financial backing to guarantee that the money invested with them will be available at the time of retirement of the annuity holder.

Mr. Chairman, my question concerns an area which was discussed earlier this afternoon. Has the minister been able to make any progress in solving the difficulty with regard to RRSPs? This afternoon the minister admitted that the problem exists. Has he given any consideration to the problems which will arise in terms of equity if he makes that change? I do not mean today, but can he give it consideration in the near future? Will the income tax system be made more equitable? Will the type of situation which I referred to this afternoon be eliminated? According to information released by Revenue Canada, in 1975 over 300 people had incomes of over $50,000 and paid no income tax. Those incomes are quite large by anyone's standard.

We always look at ways and means to improve the tax system. We are attempting to avoid as many loopholes as possible. The hon. member is referring to a scheme whereby a person who makes $50,000 takes advantage of all exemptions which exist in the law. It is not a case of this

person paying no income tax. Usually it is postponed, and so on. We attempt to avoid that situation.
Everyone can make heartbreaking cases. The situation under RRSPs has been referred to where two minors can be cut and so on. We have to overcome the problem of very large accumulations of funds tax free which, at the end of the process, could be transferred with no tax. It could be a big pipeline of tax exemptions. I should like to examine all aspects rather than attempt to solve one specific problem which perhaps could create a large loophole for others to abuse.
Dealing with the situation concerning unmatured RRSPs and dependent children, I should like to look into that. I have a lot of sympathy for the situation, but at the same time it is a departure from the present tax system. In relation to assets being transferred to children within a family because of the death of an RRSP holder, if there is some capital gains and unpaid taxes on those assets, this is the occasion for the government to take its share of what has to be paid according to the law of the land.

I would not want someone reading Hansard to have the impression that I was referring to hypothetical cases of people using various loopholes in the rules and regulations of the Income Tax Act as a way of avoiding the payment of income tax. I was not talking about hypothetical cases. This afternoon I quoted precisely from the annual report of Revenue Canada. It indicated exactly how many people were involved. I am not talking about people avoiding taxes by not reporting income. The report concerned people who avoided the payment of income taxes, despite the fact that over 300 of them had reported incomes of $50,000, $100,000 or $200,000.
In all seriousness, it would be much easier to say no to the people in low and middle income levels who want a bit of a break in the disposition of their RRSPs. It would be difficult to say to them that they are being asked to pay a pretty heavy tax because everyone is doing so. It is very difficult to indicate that to them when one realizes that there are large numbers of people who find ways of not paying income tax.
I urge the minister to look at the United States legislation which set up the Securities Exchange Commission. One of its provisions requires corporations which operate and sell shares in the United States to make public information with regard to the remunerations paid to their directors, officers and underwriters, as well as their contracts with the corporations, their bonus and profit-sharing arrangements, stock options and so on. It is standard for that information to be made public in the United States. Therefore, Americans know more about what corporate exectives are doing and what their incomes are than Canadians do. The information we require is much less and it is not given to the public. It is time for Canada to have that type of legislation in order for Canadians to know how the free enterprise system operates.

1 will not read the letter again, Mr. Chairman. In fact, I will not read any of the letter again. The

parliamentary secretary knows that all hon. members have received letters from dozens of credit unions as well as Co-op Trust, Co-op Insurance, et cetera.
The parliamentary secretary said a few minutes ago that the minister would be meeting with the credit unions, and 1 think 1 heard him aright when he said, "to reach some reasonable settlement". Once this clause is passed, Mr. Chairman, I cannot understand how the parliamentary secretary or the minister can reach some kind of settlement with the credit unions, Co-op Trust and the Registered Retirement Savings Plan holders once this becomes law, unless the Liberal government has some unique way of making changes in the way this clause reads without amending the law.

There was great encouragement in earlier budgets of a few years ago, and a lot of Canadians did so. I will just stick with term deposits, draw my compound interest, pay my income tax on the interest and stay further ahead. I am further ahead than if I were to buy these annuities which you have to buy up as introduced by the Minister of Finance, after the government brought in earlier budgets to encourage people to buy registered retirement savings plans and gave them generous tax benefits.
Without reading the letter, Mr. Chairman, in the case of a single parent who dies leaving two children, the benefit drops from $10,100 to $6,800. But to change the rules about halfway through the ball game is not fair in terms of the tax penalty after the government has spent a few years and two budgets enticing Canadians to buy registered retirement savings plans.
Surely the minister and the parliamentary secretary must be having second thoughts about clause 34. I say they have to because mail that 1 am sure all hon. members have received

indicates that people and organizations who have written cannot all be wrong. I would like to know whether the minister is prepared to withdraw clause 34. How the hell can a minister of finance agree to something different from what is in the law if he meets with these people after the clause has passed?

Later on, if he is still Minister of Finance, and after he has met with the credit unions and the Co-op Trust, if he wants to bring in another bill he is perfectly welcome to do so. Surely that is not fair.
Surely the Minister of Finance must know that. Surely he must realize that whatever his advisors told him was wrong. Surely the co-operative movement and the caisses populaires are speaking up for the tens of thousands of people who have bought these plans, on the advice of the government, with their tax incentives. And now within a matter of two or three years after these people have done that, the minister proposes to increase the tax on these plans. That is not fair ball.
Mir. Alexander: That is less than honest.
1 think the minister should tell the House tonight that once we reach ten o'clock and the bill goes through, it goes through without clause 34.

Mr. Chairman, 1 cannot give the guarantee to the hon. gentleman. I said earlier that this clause is very important because it is interrelated to the new flexibility that we are giving to the people who have bought registered retirement savings plans. We are adding via this bill a new flexibility. As 1 have said many times today, when one reaches the age of 71 only two options are available: either the individual cashed his RRSP and paid the tax in one shot at that date, using the money as he wanted, or he could buy a life annuity. With the RRIF, the program which we are introducing today, the individual will have much more flexibility. He will be able to buy another form of savings which will be called the RRIF. He will be able to spread his income over a period of years. The tax will be paid at each year's level. So this system is providing a lot of flexibility to those Canadians who bought an RRSP.
In the discussions 1 have had, from the letters 1 have received as well as from my own information, we can see some problems for holders of the unmatured RRSPs when these plans go to children or dependents. To the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and to the hon. member for Assiniboia who have made representations in that regard, I say

June 19, 1978
Income Tax Act
that I am looking into that situation. I have a lot of sympathy with this problem but I want to take a look at the implications before coming to a decision. In protecting certain circumstances I do not want to create more problems.
I might add that I have been made aware of these problems only during the last few days. I hope I will be able to come up with a solution as quickly as possible. If I can, 1 will find ways and means to do so. If there is some precedent you want to correct in midstream we can always take steps to correct it subject to later legislation. I will undertake to go to work as quickly as possible and try to resolve the situation. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in order to ensure that there is no misunderstanding with respect to comments raised by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre, I would like to say that the minister made a commitment to meet with the trust companies, credit unions and other financial institutions in trying to arrive at a reasonably satisfactory solution. At the present time no official representation has been made by the credit unions. All we have are letters sent by the individual credit unions or representations made by members from both sides of the House.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad to have the words of the parliamentary secretary. Once this clause becomes law, unless new legislation is brought in, no matter how much one agrees with the representations of credit unions, the only solution is to amend the law. It does not say much for the advisers to the Minister of Finance and the parliamentary secretary. Since the budget was brought down it has taken that time for the Co-op Trust and the credit-unions to realize what the ramifications of the legislation will be. If the minister's advisers did not follow through on what the ramifications are, he should fire those advisers.
The Minister of Finance talks about the RRIFs, the registered retirement income funds. He is a very optimistic minister. The change proposed by the minister would allow RRSP holders to establish a registered retirement income fund which would provide payments until the planholder reaches the age of 90. Now, really, Mr. Chairman, why did he not put down age 190? The RRIFs will provide continually increasing payments as long as the fund generates a return on its investment. That will tend to offset some price increases caused by inflation. Maybe that is what the minister's advisers had in mind. I do not know if there is anyone in this place who will live to age 190, except for the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the right hon. member for Prince Albert, but I just do not

accept it, and neither does the Co-op Trust and the credit unions, and I think they are probably somewhat more expert in this area than I am.
I do not think the alternative that the Minister of Finance suggests is adequate. I do not think it is sufficient to overcome or offset criticisms by the co-operative and credit union movement of what the government intends to do on this bill concerning the registered retirement savings plans. If the rules are to be changed on a long-term investment or long-term pension program, you cannot make the change and have it take effect immediately. If we are going to change the rules on something that is a long-term investment or long-term program, we cannot make the change to have effect immediately. We must not punish people who took the government's advice two or three years ago and bought these plans on the basis of long-term retirement, people who are investing for the longterm in their retirement, by three or four years later coming out with a substantially increased tax. We cannot do that once they have taken out the annuity, or if the recipient or the owner of a plan dies and the beneficiary loses as much as one third. Surely that is not fair.
I do not see how the minister or his parliamentary secretary can say that even though we pass this clause tonight, he will reach some settlement with the credit unions and the co-op trusts. The minister cannot kid me that he will meet with them one week and the next bring in a bill to amend this act. He is not kidding me or anyone else. It would save a hell of a lot of trouble if he withdrew those sections, met with those organizations and came up with some firm legislation to deal with those two matters in a way that is fair to the people who followed the advice of the government several years ago.

The hon. member should know that very often with technical problems under the present system we make an announcement that such and such a change can be made and that it will be done in the next legislation, retroactive to a date chosen by the minister. We have to do that all the time when there are difficult problems.
If we have a problem, as I suspect we have, it would solve the problem. With regard to the comment as to why we choose age 90 as being optimistic, it is a way to spread the revenues. If you choose more years than that, the revenues will be less. Income will have to be spread over a longer period of time. We want to cover most of the people who retire and choose the plan after 71. That is why age 90 is a fair number.
If a man dies before that age, a certain amount would be received the first year and another amount the second year, according to inflation. In that way it is spread. If he dies between the ages of 71 and 91, his wife can carry on until she reaches 90. Of course, if he is alone when he dies, this is included in his estate and taxed accordingly.
This is to spread the revenue. Before that there was no option. If one did not take an annuity, one had to take the cash and pay the tax at 71. If there was a substantial amount of
June 19, 1978

money, the tax was very high. In order to reduce that, we will permit them to spread the level of taxation over a period of years. That will reduce the level of tax a person has to pay.
A person also had the choice of taking a life annuity. The problem with a life annuity is that if he dies six months later, only the spouse qualifies. Other survivors do not get anything. The scheme we propose has a lot more flexibility for those who are retired and have saved money through RRSPs.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I just want to consider momentarily what we have here now. It is a most unusual situation as far as clause 34 is concerned. We have the minister stand in his place in a most unusual situation saying, in effect, that this clause is defective in some material respects. However, he is not prepared to do anything now except possibly give a vague undertaking to maybe consult with some of the people who have been making representations, such as the credit unions. He goes on to explain that we have an obligation and do not want to lose any tax money. That is the essence of what he is saying, that he does not want to lose any tax money.
If we made any changes, it might have the effect of not picking up some tax from that group of people who might derive benefits from some sensible and reasonable amendments brought forward at this time. I would never admit that.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
I do not know how else to interpret this. I do not know what to expect from this minister.
I want to bring another matter to the attention of the committee, a reference that neither I nor anyone who follows this debate would appreciate. The minister made a smart remark to the effect that, because he was speaking in French, 1 did not understand what he was talking about and therefore did not listen to him. This minister is the same as the Minister of Transport who goes across this country sowing the seeds of dissent. What kind of statement is that from the Minister of Finance? What kind of a man is that who, with a position within cabinet, continually pretends that he is wrapping himself in the flag, wanting to keep the country together, while raising great emotional debates about fighting for our country?
1 do not hold any grudge against him because his English is not perfect. I consider him as good a Canadian as I am. However, I resent these cheap, uncalled for statements that somehow, because he is speaking the other official language, 1 do not follow or care to follow what he is saying. I was going to raise a question of privilege, but I now make the point. I do not
Income Tax Act
think that anything he says or does is worthy of any sort of question of privilege.
Getting back to the point, I want to get some information from the minister. I am speaking in one of the official languages. I think he understands that. What kind of commitment do we have from the minister? Let us get down to the bare facts of this matter with regard to the question of dependents. If we are going to extend this great undertaking of the minister, and if he is going to consult with those who find a problem with this particular clause, what kind of a firm undertaking do we have?
Does he now undertake to make the appropriate changes so that dependent children will derive the benefit of not having the fund taxable in the same way as a spouse would not have it taxable in the event of death before an option is taken with regard to the RRIF or the annuity basis? Can he now undertake that those who involve themselves in RRSPs will not have to concern themselves, in the event of their death, that dependent children will find themselves with a tax situation different from that of a spouse under this provision? If he can give that undertaking, it would be something. Even if it does not have the basis of law, we would understand that the government's intention is clear, that those people who do not pay tax or withhold money for taxes would be acting upon the minister's statement in this House. How far does this undertaking go? I want to hear the minister's statement in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, I do not have to repeat what I have said. The hon. member is creating the impression that when an RRSP under the old provision was transfered to dependents, there was no tax paid. There was some tax paid. In some cases it was higher; in others it was lower. However, it was paid. There could have been income averaging, but there was some tax to be paid.
Under that system, it could be there are some circumstances which I said I would like to look into and come up with a solution. I undertook that I would do that as quickly as possible. If there is something wrong with this clause after I have analysed it thoroughly, I will undertake, as I said earlier tonight, to give notice that I will make a change, as I have done in many other instances. I will make a public announcement at the next occasion that there will be a tax bill which will amend the act to achieve that goal, and it will be done retroactively. The lawyers in the Department of National Revenue will be under notice that there will be a change to meet the requirement retroactive to that date. As a result, nobody will be off base. We have done this before and will do it again if need be.
However, I have to make sure we are not creating a loophole here. We are not dealing only with people who can accumulate $20,000 or $50,000 in RRSPs. There are some who over a long period can accumulate $300,000 upon which income tax has not been paid. The system could become a loophole for people who are at the high end of the income bracket and our readiness to give tax benefits under certain conditions does not

mean we want to give a hell of a break to people who may have accumulated $300,000.
I do not think it would be responsible for a minister of finance to act without taking such matters into consideration and receiving advice on the subject. I have received letters, as have many hon. members. But I have not received briefs from those who regularly send briefs to my department asking me to make changes. As soon as 1 reach the conclusion that something ought to be done it will be done in the fashion 1 have indicated. The truth is, the RRIF that we are creating at this moment is a hell of a new good system enabling people to exercise greater flexibility. Members opposite do not want to talk about the good aspects; they would like me to throw the baby out with the bathwater and I will not do that.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
It is amusing to hear the minister talking about these great new ideas. The suggestion that there should be more flexibility with regard to RRSPs has been put forward to the minister and his predecessors ever since I have been in this House. It was swept aside time and again with the same excuse that it was necessary to maintain the integrity of the system no matter how stupid the rule. 1 am not suggesting for a moment the minister is not making an effort to introduce greater flexibility, though perhaps he is not proceeding as fast or as far as I would like to see.
The minister tries to discount the question I put to him by saying there is not tax payable. That was not the point raised in my question at all. My point is this: after a legitimate point had been raised this afternoon by my hon. friend from Pro-vencher, the minister admitted dependent children were not in the same category as a spouse even under the existing clause. I thought he made a forceful presentation of the argument that a similar rule should apply in the case of dependents as in the case of spouses. The minister says no, so there is a fundamental difference.
There is a fundamental difference.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
The minister admits there is something wrong with this clause. He says he is prepared to enter into consultations about it. I hope those consultations will be more meaningful than the consultations with the provinces he talked about just before six o'clock. To my mind, what he said was flim-flam. On the basis of what I read in press reports and of the communique issued by the four western premiers, I would say that the hon. gentleman is not very good at consultation.
I would like to find out precisely when he proposes to amend the legislation having regard to realities about the length of this session. Nothing will really suffer if we do not give third reading to this bill before the end of June when we get out of here. We on this side of the House are prepared, as ever, to expedite good legislation, but clause 5 is a travesty, an indica-

tion of the sloppy, unprepared, unthinking and inept provision which we should be prepared to amend in committee of the whole. But debate is prematurely cut off because the minister is afraid to defend the measure clause by clause.
There have been complaints with regard to this clause and the minister has admitted it is imperfect. In answer to criticism he says: "Oh, I will consult and we can deal with it". He takes the attitude that if the government has open to it the option to err when collecting taxes at the expense of dependent children, of those who cannot defend themselves and who need help at a time of rising prices in order to maintain themselves in the event of the death of a parent, it will err on the side of continuing to collect taxes. He would prefer to maintain the integrity of the tax collection system. No social compassion is being shown by the minister.
A good case has been made by hon. members on this side of the House and, indeed, by members of the New Democratic Party. But the minister merely gives an airy-fairy promise to engage in consultations and, later, gives notice of an intention to correct any shortcomings. He gives no specific undertaking. He says he will do the best he can. "Trust in me", he says. This is not the kind of statement one would expect from a Minister of Finance with any social compassion. Will the minister undertake to engage in consultation with the parties involved to make sure he has a clause which he can defend before third reading is over? I am sure we will give unanimous consent on this side in the event of any reasonable amendment being brought forward at any stage. It is not good enough to reply to the letters we have received saying only that the minister intends to consider the problem. Will the minister assure us that the clause will be amended so as to alleviate the concern expressed by the trust companies, the caisse populaires and others across Canada, and will he hold back third reading until this has been done?

I gave my response to that suggestion earlier in reply to the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre. There is a difference between a retirement savings plan and an estate. An RRSP is not an estate. It is an accumulation of savings so that people can have income when they retire. We have to treat it like that. It is not a means by which to avoid taxes or to accumulate wealth to transmit to children or dependents. It is a system by which money can be put aside for savings so that there can be income at the time of retirement.
I think hon. members are trying to take the legislation away from its original purpose, which is to allow for money to be put aside for retirement purposes. It is not a tax loophole so that wealth can be accumulated for children or dependents. It is something else. It is a registered retirement savings plan. The words are very clear. This afternoon the hon. member for Provencher and tonight the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar have been trying to divert attention from that, and I think it has to be made very clear. All kinds of cases could be made. Some suggest that if a planholder dies, the money should go to
June 19, 1978

this family tax-free. That is not what the plan is for. It is for retirement.
I have explained ten times that previous to now when a participant in the plan reached 71, he had only two options. He could cash his RRSP in. If he had accumulated $100,000, he paid tax on $100,000 in the year he cashed it in. His other choice would have been to buy a life annuity. If he bought a life annuity and died a week later, there might be nothing left for anyone but his spouse. We considered the wife of a man who was retiring to be part of his responsibility during retirement, but if he had two children and no wife and died at 72, there might be no asset to go to the children. It was lost completely, and the profit stayed with the insurance company. We are now allowing more flexibility so that the accumulated $100,000 over a period 20 years can be withdrawn a little every year and the tax will be paid only on the amount of money taken out each year. The level of taxation will depend on the level of income each year.
Hon. members opposite are attempting to allow accumulation of wealth for estate purposes. This program does not allow for that because, let us realize, the money put into the program during a lifetime is tax-free.
Money paid into RRSPs is not subject to income tax. That money is put aside. Tax is paid when money is withdrawn from the scheme. We have decided to bring in new programs to add flexibility, but we always had in mind that the purpose of this program is to maintain income levels for retired people. The program is not meant to allow an accumulation of wealth. We should not mix the two. This afternoon the hon. member for Provencher and tonight the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar have been trying to develop it that way. They argue that the plan should be tax free. Everyone in this land would like to have to pay no taxes, but we have to maintain the important principle that RRSPs and RRIFs are schemes to maintain the incomes of people. They are not meant to build estates.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am not going to carry on much longer because I know others have points to make.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
1 know hon. members on the government side must be embarrassed to think about supporting the Minister of Finance in this proposition. It is a very simple proposition. The minister says that the scheme applies to spouses, but he cannot bring himself to extend it to dependent children.
If every hon. member on the government side would canvass their own personal situation-and I am not now thinking of their constituents-those who have dependent children might ask themselves why the plan should not include them. If the plan now goes as far as including spouses, why not dependent children? Perhaps the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre is right. If this government stays in power much longer, the rate of taxation will be so high by the time we withdraw our RRSPs that it would be better to pay tax on our incomes and just let our money earn interest.
Income Tax Act
However, I ask hon. members opposite to consider the extension of this principle and to put pressure on the minister to make a firm declaration that he will bring in an appropriate amendment to extend this plan to dependent children. That is a social aim. That will not cause the government to lose all its income, even this government with its spending habits. We have received a good lecture from the minister, but the point I want to make and the point which was made by the hon. member for Provencher this afternoon is that this would not be an overwhelming concession on the part of the government. All I am asking is that the government accept this basic principle.
I will not stand here and waste the remainder of the evening talking to unyielding ears. There are important clauses here, but the minister does not seem to have the compassion or the interest to do anything about this important proposition. I want him to understand what considerations are moving people on this side to make this kind of representation. It is not in any partisan political sense but in the interests of all those dependent children who might be in this unfortunate situation. I hope the minister will give serious thought, before this bill is read the third time, to changing his mind on this.

Mr. Chairman, the minister was implying that we on this side were suggesting that we should have a tax-free situation as far as RRSPs are concerned. Up until now taxation with respect to the plan has been certain. Attempts are being made in this legislation to change the system of taxation for this plan in midstream. All we are asking is that the minister do what he said when he responded to the hon. member for Dauphin on June 12. He said there would be no changes in taxation for RRSPs because people have purchased plans over the years based on the certainty that there were certain rules and regulations.
Now, half-way through, the minister is changing the system of taxation. All we are asking is that he understand that when people entered into this plan they knew what the taxation liability would be. If at some future time we want to create a situation whereby tax liability will be different, that is fine; but let us tell people who have purchased these plans up until now that there will be no change in the law as it existed for them when they purchased their plans. If the minister wants to discuss this matter with credit unions, trust companies and other institutions with regard to the future, that is fine; but let there be some certainty with respect to the plans which exist at the present time so that there will be no misunderstandings.

Mr. Chairman, many times I have indicated to the committee that I have sympathy for the dependents of participants in registered retirement savings plans, but I doubt very much whether the dependents of participants over 71 have very much need. Quite a lot of money can be accumulated under RRSPs. If there is a need there, I doubt it is very frequent because when you reach the age at which you benefit from an RRIF, there can be a lot of money accumulated in the fund but there are very few people with dependent children in that category. So this is not a common occurrence we would be faced with, though there could be an exceptional situation. For

Mr. Chairman, 1 rise on a question of privilege. I want to remind the minister that there are many virile people in this country. In fact, I have three constituents over 80 years old who draw old age pension and family allowance at the same time.
That is why I said I would like to help those valuable persons.

Mr. Chairman, I think it must be obvious to members of the House that the Minister of Finance is absolutely inflexible with respect to the requests we have been putting forth concerning an RRSP should a person die with one of those plans in force. So I propose to ask the minister a few questions about another subclause under clause 34.
I refer the minister to clause 34(9) which appears at page 40 of the bill. This is the provision in which it is proposed to limit to age 60 the starting date for life annuity payments under the matured RRSP. I recommend that the minister consider withdrawing that proposal. I say this because, before putting my direct question to the minister, I think he would agree that under the present plan there is no minimum age limit, nor has there been any such limitation since the RRSP was introduced into the Income Tax Act back in 1957. So for some 20-odd years there has been no minimum age at which a person can rollover or in some other way deal with the funds which he has in an RRSP. Would the minister consider withdrawing his proposal for a new minimum age limit so far as the RRSP is concerned?

Perhaps, as usual, I will read the technical explanation first and following that I will deal with the points made by the hon. member.
In subparagraph 146(2)(b)(iii) the change introduced the new provision regarding the time at which payments of retirement income out of RRSP must start. Retirement income must commence at some time after the annuitant becomes 60 and before the end of the year in which he becomes 72 years of age. RRSPs were introduced as a tax assisted savings plan for the purpose of providing an income in retirement for those who did not have access to a pension plan. Too often only the short term tax saving aspects are emphasized. The age 60 provision emphasizes the essential nature of these plans without impeding their continued widespread use. Since retirement before the age of 60 is actually rare, although widely discussed, it enables the retirement nature to be emphasized with the minimum of inconvenience. For the rare case, where the

money is needed, the plan can still be used to provide retirement income before the age of 60, but the technique is somewhat different.
To answer the hon. member as to why there should be a minimum age, let me say to him that it is to illustrate the point I was making earlier with regard to the confusion that is developing in the minds of some people at this time. People seem to forget that those are tax deductions or incentives we are giving to individuals to save money for their retirement. Now it seems to be drifting into something else. People seem to think it is a way of accumulating wealth without paying taxes.
To illustrate this clearly, we are designating the age of 60 as the starting age for RRSP. 1 do not know whether 60 is too late or too early. We used to talk about retirement at age 65 and then we wanted to reduce the age of retirement. Now there are people in this land who argue that we should depart from the practice of making people retire at a certain age. My point is that we want to make it clear-because 1 detected earlier in this debate and on other occasions the danger that people may think that RRSPs are a way to accumulate wealth-that it is a retirement savings plan. That is why we put the age of 60 there, but it is not an essential provision.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the minister's answer, in which he said we were confused concerning the taxability of these lump sum amounts which end up in RRSPs, I would like to put three examples to the minister and ask him how he distinguishes among the deferred income plans to which I will refer in that there is no minimum age in any of the three and yet, for reasons about which 1 am not clear, he hopes to introduce the minimum age in the case of RRSPs.
The first example I put to the minister is that the current requirement under the Income Tax Act is that the maturity date for an RRSP must be on or before attainment of age 71. We agree on that. There is no minimum age limitation, nor has there been any such limitation since 1957. I ask the minister how he distinguishes between the present position with respect to an RRSP and, for example, the deferred profit sharing plans? The Income Tax Act has followed the same pattern as RRSPs; that is, it provides that benefits be paid out not later than at the age of 71 but that there be no minimum age. Why is the RRSP, if amended as the minister suggests, different from the present Income Tax Act provision with respect to deferred profit sharing plans?

The purpose of the profit sharing plans is not necessarily retirement income. It could serve as a retirement instrument but this is not the main purpose of the plan. The philosophy of RRSP is quite different from that of deferred profit sharing plans. That is why there is no minimum age requirement in the case of deferred profit sharing plans.

If that is the case, then I will be most curious to find out the minister's reason for the minimum age in my second example. The Income Tax Act does not provide any minimum age for commencement of a pension under an employee pension plan, but Revenue Canada has issued infor-

mation circular 72-13R4 which stipulates that normal retirement age under a pension plan should not be earlier than age 60 but allows for payment of pensions at an earlier date under certain circumstances. These circumstances include retirement at age 55 after 25 years of service or retirement after 30 years of service regardless of age. Can the minister distinguish why, in the case of the information circular to which I have referred, it is permissible to have these plans with regard to people who wish to retire before age 60, but under the registered retirement savings plans arbitrarily the minimum age is 60?

Mr. Chairman, as I said earlier about the last proposal made by the hon. member, he is alluding to the age of 60. Of course, as concerns pension plans, we have provided more flexibility to allow those who have now reached 60 to benefit from the plans in certain circumstances for various reasons. But as regards the plans called RRSPs, we have set the minimum age at 60 for the reason that I have mentioned on several occasions in committee. More and more these plans are being considered not as savings plans which provide you with money for your retirement, but as plans which enable you to avoid paying normal taxes throughout the years. You have only to read the advertisements in the newspapers or the propaganda made by those who sell pension plans. They very rarely mention pensions, and very often they talk mostly of the pension plans as a means to avoid paying income tax. This is one of the problems that we want to avoid. We must not forget the purpose of this type of plan which is to save money for one's retirement. If we let people get too far away from this purpose, one day our program will finally be considered by the public as strictly a means to avoid paying normal income taxes. This is one of the problems which we must always face in such programs. We must ensure that the main purpose is not lost in the evolution of such plans because people could finally so much abuse what is good for other purposes that the whole program would have to be eliminated in the end because it would no longer meet the original objectives.
In the circumstances, we must be very cautious, and I believe that we have been wise to choose the age of 60 in the case of RRSPs. If we discover that this is too restrictive, we can always change the program, but I cannot see why it would not be important to come back to the purpose for which this program was created and set the minimum age at 60.

I understand what the minister is saying, that presumably at some stage a plan should be subject to equitable tax. The minister is not consistent. In private pension plans, which have the advantage of tax deferral, Revenue Canada is willing to allow those plans to be operative, in the case of a person working for 30 years, at any age, and in the case of a person working for 25 years, at 55 years of age. Notwithstand-
Income Tax Act
ing the fact that it is acceptable to allow those plans to be operative at ages lower than 60, why is the department arbitrarily harsh in respect of those who have participated in RRSPs?

There is no flexibility in pension plans as there is in RRSPs. A person can withdraw any portion of his RRSP before age 60, whenever he requires the money. It is not a question of the funds being locked in.
At which point he is required to pay the tax.

For example, if a person has accumulated $100,000, in RRSPs, at any time when he needs money, he can arrange to take $5,000 out of the plan if he wants. He can pay tax any year he wants at that level, and he is taxed according to his income in that year. It is normal, for we must remember that he was not taxed in the first place.
As 1 explained earlier, the purpose of this scheme was to make funds available at the time of retirement. If a person withdraws any portion of it at age 50, he must pay taxes according to his income at that time. That is fair, because at the time his money was put into the RRSP he was not required to pay tax on it.
RRSPs are designed for retirement purposes. Before the age of 60, a person has a lot of flexibility in his plan. He can withdraw the money or any portion of it. But that is not the case under pension plans.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to emphasize that pension plans can be discontinued. My third example is the case of employee profit-sharing plans. Revenue Canada issued Information Circular 71-1R. It requires simply that the normal retirement age for payment of benefits be defined in the plan, but that no minimum age is required. In these three very relevant examples, why is the department willing to be flexible as to the operative age, whereas under RRSPs arbitrarily the minimum age is 60?
I would like to mention a few very brief examples of genuine hardship which will result for people who are counting on the proceeds from registered retirement savings plans. They will not be able to participate because of the arbitrary 60-year figure which the minister has come up with.
The hon. member must understand that between the ages of 60 and 71 a person can transfer his RRSP into an RRIF.
I am dealing with under age 60.

Under 60 a person can withdraw any portion of his RRSP, but it cannot be transferred to an RRIF. He can use that money in order to pay his taxes or do whatever he wants. It was necessary to have a minimum age for a person wanting to transfer his RRSPs into RRIFs.
The purpose of RRIF is to ensure, when a person reaches retirement, that he is not forced to take all his RRSP savings and pay his taxes in one shot, and to ensure that he is not

forced to buy a life annuity. We want to provide some flexibility for people who have RRSP savings.
Because RRSPs will be flowing now into RRIFs, it was necessary to establish a minimum age. Otherwise, there would have been a complete confusion. We should not make the program inoperative or more difficult. We want to help people with RRSPs to save money, in order for them to have cash to add to their retirement incomes.

In the case of an individual who encounters a permanent impairment of health or other factors which force him to adjust to a limited work schedule and a reduced income, perhaps it would be logical for him to convert his RRSP into an immediate annuity payment in order to supplement his inadequate income. Such a person will not be able to do that, if this minimum 60-year requirement goes through, if in fact he is less than 60 years of age. Why cannot that flexibility be offered?

That person could achieve exactly the same purpose if he withdrew a portion of his RRSP every year. If he feels he requires $3,000 more, because he has lost his capacity of earning at age 55, he can decide to withdraw that amount from his RRSP. Also he will pay the tax on this amount according to his level of tax at age 55. That is quite simple. He can do that whenever he wants. He is not penalized by this scheme.

Mr. Chairman, let me put the situation to the minister in which there has been a premature death. Under the present RRSP the law is flexible, and, I would suggest, well suited to emergencies of this kind, because a surviving spouse can now roll-over the deceased's RRSP into his or her own RRSP.
